do.text: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit and keeps your changes staged. If you already pushed it, use git revert HEAD instead.

commands.title: Discard changes in a file
phrases: how (do i|to) (discard|throw away) (my|local) changes in git

do.text: git restore <file> throws away unstaged changes to that file; git restore . does it for every file. It can't be undone.
git restore --staged <file> unstages it and keeps your edits.
git switch -c <name> creates a branch and switches to it. On older Git: git checkout -b <name>.

commands.title: Delete a branch
phrases: how (do i|to) delete a git branch

do.text: git branch -d <name> deletes a merged local branch; -D forces it. For the remote one: git push origin --delete <name>.

commands.title: Rename a branch
phrases: how (do i|to) rename a git branch

do.text: git branch -m <new-name> renames the branch you're on.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate shows a compact history with branches.
git stash saves your uncommitted changes and cleans the working tree; git stash pop brings them back. git stash list shows what's saved.
git commit --amend lets you change the last commit's message or content. Avoid it if you've already pushed.

commands.title: Set name and email
phrases: how (do i|to) set my git (name|username|email|name and email)

do.text: git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email you@example.com.
Open each conflicted file, keep the right code between the <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers and delete the markers. Then git add the files and git commit (or git rebase --continue).
git fetch, then git rebase origin/main. Fix conflicts, git add them, git rebase --continue. git rebase --abort puts everything back.

commands.title: Fetch vs pull
phrases: what is the difference between git fetch and [git] pull

do.text: git fetch downloads new commits without touching your files. git pull fetches and then merges (or rebases) them into your branch.
git remote -v shows it; git remote set-url origin <new-url> changes it.

commands.title: Ignore files
phrases: how (do i|to) (ignore files in git|use gitignore)

do.text: List patterns in a .gitignore file at the repo root, like node_modules/ or *.log. Files already tracked need git rm --cached <file> once.

commands.title: Cherry-pick
phrases: how (do i|to) cherry pick a commit

do.text: git cherry-pick <commit> copies that one commit onto your current branch.
git tag v1.0.0, then git push origin v1.0.0. Annotated: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "message".
git diff shows unstaged changes; git diff --staged shows what will be committed.
git revert <commit> makes a new commit that undoes it — safe on shared branches, unlike reset.
git rebase -i HEAD~3, then change pick to squash on the commits to fold in. Or choose squash merge on the pull request.

commands.title: Find the commit that broke it
phrases: how (do i|to) find (the|which) commit [that] broke (it|something|the build)

do.text: git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good <old-commit>, then test each commit Git checks out and mark good or bad until it names the culprit. git bisect reset when done.
git reflog lists everywhere HEAD has been. Find the hash, then git switch -c rescue <hash> to bring it back.
git clone <url> copies the repository into a new folder. Add a folder name at the end to choose it.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com". Then paste the contents of the .pub file into GitHub, Settings, SSH and GPG keys.
docker ps shows running containers; docker ps -a shows all of them, stopped ones too.

commands.title: Clean up Docker
phrases: how (do i|to) (clean up|free space in) docker

do.text: docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks and dangling images. Add -a to remove every unused image too.
docker logs -f <container> follows its output; --tail 100 shows only the last 100 lines.

commands.title: Shell into a container
phrases: how (do i|to) (get a shell|open a terminal) (in|inside) a [docker] container

do.text: docker exec -it <container> sh — or bash if the image has it.

commands.title: Build an image
phrases: how (do i|to) build a docker image

do.text: docker build -t <name> . builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current folder.
docker run -p 8080:80 <image> maps port 8080 on your PC to port 80 inside the container.
docker compose up -d starts everything in compose.yaml in the background; docker compose down stops and removes it; docker compose logs -f follows the logs.
npm init -y creates a package.json with the defaults.

commands.title: Install a dev dependency
phrases: how (do i|to) install a dev dependency

do.text: npm install --save-dev <package>, or the short form npm i -D <package>.
npm outdated lists newer versions; npm update updates within your version ranges. For major versions, install them explicitly.
npm audit lists known vulnerabilities; npm audit fix applies the safe updates. Read what --force would change before using it.
npm ci installs exactly what's in package-lock.json and deletes node_modules first — the right choice for CI and clean builds.
npx runs a package's command without installing it globally, like npx create-vite@latest.

commands.title: Version ranges
phrases: what (does|do) (the caret|caret|tilde|the tilde) mean in package json

do.text: Versions are major.minor.patch. ^1.2.3 allows minor and patch updates; ~1.2.3 allows only patch updates.
python -m venv .venv creates it. Activate it on Windows with .venv\Scripts\activate, on Mac or Linux with source .venv/bin/activate.
pip freeze > requirements.txt saves your installed packages; pip install -r requirements.txt installs them.
python -m pip install --upgrade pip.
python -m http.server 8000 serves the current folder at http://localhost:8000.
With Ruff: ruff format . formats the code and ruff check --fix fixes lint problems.

commands.title: Run tests with pytest

do.text: pytest runs tests in test_*.py files. pytest -k name runs matching tests, -x stops at the first failure, -q keeps it quiet.
uv is a fast Python package manager: uv venv makes an environment, uv pip install <pkg> installs into it, uv run <script> runs with dependencies.

commands.title: Find what's using a port

do.text: In PowerShell: Get-Command <name>. In Command Prompt: where <name>. On Linux or Mac: which <name>.

do.text: grep -rn "text" . searches every file below this folder. In PowerShell: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File | Select-String text. Or install ripgrep and run rg text.

do.text: Open Terminal as administrator and run wsl --install. Restart, then open Ubuntu from the Start menu and create your Linux user.
winget search <app> finds it, winget install <id> installs it, and winget upgrade --all updates everything.
kubectl get pods lists pods; kubectl logs <pod> shows logs; kubectl describe pod <pod> explains why it's failing; kubectl apply -f file.yaml creates or updates resources.
The browser blocked the response because the server didn't allow your page's origin. Fix it on the server by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your site, or call the API from your own backend.
A JWT is a signed token in three base64 parts: header, payload and signature. Anyone can read the payload; the signature only proves it wasn't changed. Don't put secrets in it.

commands.title: REST vs GraphQL
phrases: (what is the difference between|compare) rest and graphql

do.text: REST has many URLs, each returning a fixed shape. GraphQL has one endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs.

do.text: SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT 10 in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite; SELECT TOP 10 ... in SQL Server.
INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, with blanks where nothing matches. FULL JOIN keeps everything from both.

commands.title: Count per group
phrases: how (do i|to) count rows per (group|category) in sql

do.text: SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY category; add HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to keep only repeated ones.

do.text: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table_name (column); index the columns you filter, join or sort on often.
\d is a digit, \w a word character, \s a space, . any character. * means zero or more, + one or more, ? optional. ^ is the start, $ the end, and (…) groups.

commands.title: .env files
phrases: what (is|are) [a] (dot env file|dot env files|env files)

do.text: .env files hold settings like API keys. Never commit them: add .env to .gitignore and share an .env.example with blank values instead.

phrases: what (do i|to) do if i leaked (an|a) (api key|secret)

do.text: Revoke or rotate the key at its provider right away — deleting the commit isn't enough, because it may already be copied. Then remove it from the code and use an environment variable.
GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part of something, DELETE removes. GET should never change data.
Big O describes how work grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving each step, O(n) one pass, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n²) nested loops.

commands.title: TCP vs UDP

do.text: TCP is reliable and ordered (web, email, files). UDP is faster with no delivery guarantee (video calls, games, DNS).

commands.title: Find MCP servers on GitHub
phrases: is there an mcp server for {q}

do.text: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI apps plug into tools and data — files, GitHub, databases, websites — through small programs called MCP servers. Echo uses MCP servers for its AI, and is one itself.
An MCP server is a small program that offers tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts to an AI app, over standard input/output or HTTP.

commands.title: Tools, resources and prompts
phrases: (what is the difference between|explain) [mcp] tools resources and prompts

do.text: Tools are actions the AI can call, like search or create issue. Resources are data it can read, like a file. Prompts are ready-made instructions the user can pick.

commands.title: stdio vs HTTP
phrases: (what is the difference between|explain) stdio and http [mcp] transport[s]

do.text: stdio servers run on your PC as a program the app starts. Streamable HTTP servers run anywhere and are reached by URL, often with a token.

commands.title: Test an MCP server
phrases: how (do i|to) test an mcp server

do.text: Run npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector, point it at your server's command or URL, then list and call its tools in the browser.

commands.title: Build an MCP server in Python
phrases: how (do i|to) (build|write|make) an mcp server in python

do.text: pip install "mcp[cli]", then: from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP; mcp = FastMCP("demo"); put @mcp.tool() on a typed function; call mcp.run(). Add it to Echo with its command.

commands.title: Build an MCP server in TypeScript
phrases: how (do i|to) (build|write|make) an mcp server in (typescript|javascript|node)

do.text: npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod, create an McpServer, register tools with a schema, and connect it with StdioServerTransport.

An MCP server can do whatever its code does, so add servers only from sources you trust. Echo runs read-only tools freely and asks you before any tool that can change things, unless you've trusted that server.

commands.title: What does trusting a server mean?
phrases: what does trusted mean for mcp

do.text: A trusted MCP server's tools run without asking you each time. Ready-made read-only servers start trusted; everything else asks first. Say “stop trusting the … tools” to undo.

commands.title: What can Echo's MCP server do?
phrases: what can [the] echo mcp server do
what tools does echo (offer|give) other ai apps

do.text: Echo's MCP server lets apps like Claude or Cursor control this PC: run any Echo command, find commands, open apps and links, type, press keys, look at the screen, click and scroll — with on-PC confirmations for risky steps.

commands.title: Add an MCP server by hand
phrases: how (do i|to) add (my own|a custom|any) mcp server

do.text: Say “manage my MCP servers”, or open Settings, MCP servers, and add a command (for stdio) or a URL (for HTTP). Or say “import my MCP servers” to copy the ones from Claude, Cursor or VS Code.

do.text: Wi-Fi is internet from a router at home or a shop. Mobile data comes from your SIM card and uses your plan's data. Wi-Fi is usually cheaper for videos.

commands.title: Book a gas cylinder
phrases: how (do i|to) book a gas cylinder

do.text: Call your gas agency's booking number, use WhatsApp booking, or the Indane, HP Gas or Bharat Gas app with your registered mobile number. Many UPI apps can book it too.

commands.title: Send a voice message
phrases: how (do i|to) send a voice (message|note) [on whatsapp]

do.text: In the WhatsApp chat, press and hold the microphone button, speak, then let go to send. Slide left to cancel.

commands.title: Group video call

commands.title: Share my location
